power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < 0.05", Text = "Black and white markers indicate reported effects that did (black) and did not (white) differ significantly (p < 0.05) from the corresponding expected effect. .064 (.006; .122)* .008 (-.017; .033) -.007 (-.021; .007) .013 (-.009; .035) Ind.M1."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. report: Below, we describe some best coding practices and give the results of automatic evaluation of these practices in the code files below. This check may miss things or produce false positives if your scripts are less typical.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("File Name" = "SCAM_Script.R", "% Comments" = "54%", "Missing Files" = 0L, "Absolute Paths" = 0L, "Code Between Libraries" = NA_integer_), row.names = 1L, class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ```
#### Code Comments
Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.
#### Missing Files
All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.
#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Libraries / Imports
Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.
#### Packages / Dependencies
The code files load 1 distinct package/library: lavaan. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).
#### Reproducible Environment

No `renv.lock` file, `sessionInfo()`/`session_info()` record, or `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an `renv.lock` (via the `renv` package), a `sessionInfo()` text dump, or a `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin alongside the code.
#### Parsable code

info.title: Shared Cause Adjusted Mediation (SCAM): Introduction of method with empirical applications

text.text: A genuine mediated effect, also called an indirect effect, is the part of the relationship between a predictor (X) and an outcome (Y) that operates through a third variable, called a mediator (M).
However, estimated mediated effects do not prove genuine mediation as they only require variables to be correlated and correlations may be due to confounding.
Here, I propose adjusting for effects that are expected if the predictor, outcome, and mediator(s) share a common latent cause.

In an application of this method on four studies using serial mediation analyses, only 5 of 24 (21%) reported effects remained statistically significant after such adjustment for a shared latent cause.
A genuine mediated effect, also called an indirect effect, is the part of the relationship between a predictor (X) and an outcome (Y) that operates through a third variable, called a mediator (M).
However, an estimated mediated effect does not necessarily imply an active mechanism.
The estimated effect could, for example, be due to spurious correlations due to confounding by a shared cause.

As an example, if three measures of depression correlate to individuals' general level of depression as in Figure 1, the mediated effect of D1 (predictor) on D3 (outcome) via D2 (mediator) would equal b = 0.25.
text.formatted: As an example, if three measures of depression correlate to individuals' general level of depression as in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, the mediated effect of D1 (predictor) on D3 (outcome) via D2 (mediator) would equal b = 0.25.

text.text: The same mediated effect would be seen for any other combination of the three variables as predictor, outcome, and mediator.
It has been argued that correlations between various psychological measures may be due to a shared latent cause, similar to the example in Figure 1.
text.formatted: It has been argued that correlations between various psychological measures may be due to a shared latent cause, similar to the example in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: This has, for example, been proposed for cognitive abilities [1], personality traits [2], measures of psychopathology [3, 4], and selfevaluations [5, 6].
text.formatted: This has, for example, been proposed for cognitive abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>, personality traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>, measures of psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>, and selfevaluations <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>.

text.text: Impact by a shared latent cause would mean that many reported mediated effects in the psychological literature may, just like in Figure 1, be spurious.
text.formatted: Impact by a shared latent cause would mean that many reported mediated effects in the psychological literature may, just like in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, be spurious.

text.text: Due to this potential for spuriousness and to increase analytic rigor, I propose that estimated mediated effects may/should be compared with and adjusted for effects that could be expected if the measures are indicators of a shared latent cause.

If a mediated effect can be accounted for by a shared latent cause of the predictor, the outcome, and the mediator(s), caution is advised and strong claims about the presence of mediation should be avoided.
A parallel can be drawn to estimations of crosslagged effects, e.g., in cross-lagged panel models (CLPM).

If we replace D1, D2, and D3 in Figure 1 by X1 (predictor at baseline), Y1 (outcome at baseline), and Y2 (subsequent score on outcome), the crosslagged effect of X1 on Y2 adjusting for Y1 would equal b = 0.39.
text.formatted: If we replace D1, D2, and D3 in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> by X1 (predictor at baseline), Y1 (outcome at baseline), and Y2 (subsequent score on outcome), the crosslagged effect of X1 on Y2 adjusting for Y1 would equal b = 0.39.

text.text: If unaware of the true data generating process, many researchers in psychology might be tempted to conclude, based on this effect, that X causes a subsequent increase in Y. However, as the effect is spurious, this conclusion would be a type-1 error.
Bias in estimated cross-lagged effects has been pointed out [e.g., 7, 8].
text.formatted: Bias in estimated cross-lagged effects has been pointed out [e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: For increased analytic rigor, researchers have developed the randomintercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM), where autoregressive and cross-lagged effects are estimated while adjusting for individuals' stable trait-like levels on the constructs [7].
text.formatted: For increased analytic rigor, researchers have developed the randomintercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM), where autoregressive and cross-lagged effects are estimated while adjusting for individuals' stable trait-like levels on the constructs <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: My proposed method is, in a way, to mediation analyses what RI-CLPM is to CLPM.

The objective of the present study was to introduce estimation of Shared Cause Adjusted Mediation (SCAM) by applying the method to four recently published studies suggesting the presence of mediation.
The scrutinized studies Selection of the four scrutinized studies followed a convenience procedure.
I searched for studies using serial mediation published in Frontiers in Psychology, a journal that I know publishes a lot of studies using this method.
I picked four recent studies that are relatively widely cited.

Serial (also called "chain" or "sequential") mediation analyses involve models where a predictor has, for example, an effect on an outcome directly as well as indirectly via a first mediator (X → M1 → Y), a second mediator (X → M2 → Y), and serially via both mediators (X → M1 → M2 → Y) (Table 1).
text.formatted: Serial (also called "chain" or "sequential") mediation analyses involve models where a predictor has, for example, an effect on an outcome directly as well as indirectly via a first mediator (X → M1 → Y), a second mediator (X → M2 → Y), and serially via both mediators (X → M1 → M2 → Y) (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: All predictors, outcomes, and mediators in the four 1 . g.
. studies were measured with self-rating Likert scales, except the predictor in Wang et al., which was measured as self-reported time spent on physical activity.
All direct, mediated, and total effects of X on Y in the four studies were statistically significant.
Authors of all four studies interpreted results in quasi-causal terms, suggesting, for example, that their findings were relevant for policy recommendations.
Such suggestions and recommendations make no sense unless associations are assumed to be causal.

Our analyses followed these steps: (1) The model in Figure 2A, where the predictor, outcome, and mediators were specified as indicators of a shared latent cause, was fitted to the correlation matrix reported in the scrutinized study; (2) The model-implied correlations between predictor, outcome, and mediators from the previous step were extracted and saved; (3) The serial mediation model in Figure 2B, identical to the model analyzed in the scrutinized studies, was fitted to the matrix of model-implied correlations; (4) The size of indirect (i.e., mediated), direct, and total effects in this serial mediation model were estimated.

text.text: These correspond to expected effects if data was generated by the shared latent cause model in Figure 2A; (5) Effects and their standard errors reported in the scrutinized study, and effects and standard errors estimated in step 4, were Fisher z-transformed; (6) A Z-value for the difference between the Fisher-transformed effect reported in the scrutinized study (zβo) and implied by the shared latent cause model (zβi) was estimated with Equation 1 (where zSEo and zSEi are standard errors of the reported and implied effects, respectively); (7) A p-value corresponding to the Z-value in step 6 was estimated, as well as a confidence interval of the the difference between reported and implied effects; (8) For reporting, the shared latent cause adjusted effect (i.e., the difference in the numerator in Equation 1) and the confidence interval of this effect (difference) were inverse Fisher-transformed back to betacoefficients.

text.text: Moreover, shared latent cause adjusted effects, i.e., the difference between observed and expected effects, are reported in
Table 2.
Of 24 evaluated reported effects, 10 differed significantly from effects predicted by a shared latent cause model, 5 in Wu et al., 3 in Yue et al., 2 in Xiong et al., and none in Wang et al.

Of these 10 statistically significant shared latent cause adjusted effects, 5 were stronger than expected (e.g., 4 of the 5 significant effects in Wu et al.) and 5 were weaker (i.e., closer to zero)  than expected (e.g., all 3 significant effects in Yue et al.)
As argued above, many reported mediated effects in the psychological literature may be spurious due to impact by some shared latent cause of the predictor, outcome, and mediator(s).
Here, I propose estimating shared cause adjusted effects, i.e., the difference between observed effects and expected effects if data was generated by a model including a single shared latent cause.
If these adjusted effects are non-significant, caution is advised and decisive conclusions of genuine effects should probably be postponed.
I believe that this method may add some much-needed rigor to mediation analyses in psychological research.
When applying this method on four studies using serial mediation analyses, 14 of 24 (58%) indirect, direct, and total effects were non-significant.
The remaining 10 effects were evenly split between effects that were stronger and weaker than expected.

This suggested, for example, that a potential decreasing impact of self-rated physical activity on negative emotions, both totally and via exercise selfefficacy, actually was weaker, and hence less important, than would be expected if data was generated by a latent shared cause.
This would correspond to a situation where a treatment group experiences a significantly worse outcome than a control group.
The only study that survived scrutiny [11] suggested an increasing effect of internet addiction on academic procrastination, partly mediated by self-control.
text.formatted: The only study that survived scrutiny <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> suggested an increasing effect of internet addiction on academic procrastination, partly mediated by self-control.

text.text: However, although surviving adjustment for a shared latent cause, these effects are still correlational and should not be interpreted as decisive evidence of causality (see below).
The proposed method of estimating shared cause adjusted effects cannot convey irrefutable evidence of causality or lack thereof.

Failure of effects to survive adjustment for a shared latent cause does not prove that data was generated by a shared latent cause model, like the one in Figure 2A, and that the effects, therefore, are spurious.
text.formatted: Failure of effects to survive adjustment for a shared latent cause does not prove that data was generated by a shared latent cause model, like the one in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2A</ref>, and that the effects, therefore, are spurious.

text.text: The more limited conclusion to be drawn is that such data generation and spuriousness of effects cannot be ruled out.
In the other direction, surviving adjustment for a shared latent cause does not prove effects to be genuinely causal.
Here, the more limited conclusion to be drawn is that effects cannot be accounted for by a single shared latent variable.
It is, for example, possible that the effects could be accounted for by a model with two separate, but correlated, latent variables.
It should be noted that the proposed method shares these limitations, i.e., inability to prove the presence or lack of causality, with other methods Figure 3.

text.text: Although adding analytic rigor, no statistical model can replace randomized controlled trials (RCT) as the gold standard for causal inference.
As mentioned above, selection of the four scrutinized studies followed a convenience procedure.

Hence, the present results, e.g., that only 21% (5 of 24) of the evaluated effects survived adjustment for a shared cause, cannot be generalized to the population of effects reported in the literature.
Here, it is important to note that reporting generalizable results was not an objective of the present study.
Estimated mediated effects do not prove genuine mediation as they only require variables to be correlated and correlations may be due to confounding.
Here, I propose estimating effects that are adjusted for effects that are expected if the predictor, outcome, and mediator(s) share a common latent cause.
This would add some muchneeded analytic rigor to mediation analyses in the psychological literature.
